content: Exercise has been shown to offer numerous health benefits and has been proposed as a potential treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea, commonly referred to as period pain. However, the evidence supporting its effectiveness in alleviating this condition remains inconclusive. This review aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of exercise as a treatment for women experiencing primary dysmenorrhoea. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility specialised register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, AMED, and CINAHL, covering studies from their inception to July 2019. Additionally, two clinical trial registries were searched up to March 2019, and reference lists of previous systematic reviews were manually examined. The inclusion criteria required studies to randomise women with moderate-to-severe primary dysmenorrhoea to either an exercise intervention or a comparator group, such as no treatment, attention control, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or oral contraceptive pills. Cross-over studies and cluster-randomised trials were excluded. Two independent reviewers selected eligible studies, assessed their risk of bias, and extracted relevant data. Missing information was sought from study authors. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The primary outcomes of interest were menstrual pain intensity and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included overall menstrual symptoms, use of rescue analgesic medication, restriction of daily activities, absence from work or school, and quality of life. A total of 12 trials involving 854 women were included in the review, with 10 trials (754 women) contributing data to the meta-analysis. Nine of these trials compared exercise with no treatment, while one trial compared exercise with NSAIDs. No studies compared exercise with attention control or oral contraceptive pills. The exercise interventions included low-intensity activities such as stretching, core strengthening, or yoga, as well as high-intensity activities like Zumba or aerobic training. None of the studies utilised resistance training. When comparing exercise to no treatment, the evidence suggests that exercise may significantly reduce menstrual pain intensity. The standard mean difference (SMD) was -1.86 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -2.06 to -1.66) based on nine randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving 632 participants. This corresponds to a reduction of approximately 25 mm on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS), which is likely to be clinically meaningful. However, the quality of evidence was rated as low. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether exercise affected the rate of adverse events. Similarly, it is uncertain whether exercise reduces overall menstrual symptoms, such as back pain or fatigue, as measured by the Moos Menstrual Distress Questionnaire (MMDQ). One RCT (n = 120) reported a mean difference (MD) of -33.16 (95% CI: -40.45 to -25.87) for overall menstrual symptoms, but the evidence was of very low quality. The impact of exercise on mental quality of life (MD 4.40, 95% CI: 1.59 to 7.21; 1 RCT, n = 55) and physical quality of life (MD 3.40, 95% CI: -1.68 to 8.48; 1 RCT, n = 55) was also uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. No studies reported on the effects of exercise on daily activity restrictions or absence from work or school. When comparing exercise to NSAIDs, the evidence is very limited. One RCT (n = 122) compared exercise to mefenamic acid and found that exercise may reduce menstrual pain intensity (MD -7.40, 95% CI: -8.36 to -6.44), but the evidence was of very low quality. The same study reported no clear difference in the use of rescue analgesic medication (risk ratio [RR] 1.77, 95% CI: 1.21 to 2.60) or absence from work or school (RR 1.00, 95% CI: 0.49 to 2.03). No data were available on adverse events, overall menstrual symptoms, daily activity restrictions, or quality of life in this comparison. The authors concluded that current evidence, although of low quality, suggests that regular exercise performed for 45 to 60 minutes, at least three times per week, may lead to a clinically significant reduction in menstrual pain intensity of approximately 25 mm on a 100 mm VAS. The included studies generally required participants to engage in exercise throughout the month, with some advising against exercise during menstruation. Given the overall health benefits of exercise and its low risk of adverse effects in the general population, women may consider incorporating exercise into their management of menstrual pain, either as a standalone intervention or in combination with other treatments such as NSAIDs. However, it remains unclear whether the benefits of exercise persist after discontinuation or whether similar effects are observed in women over the age of 25. Further research is needed, employing validated outcome measures, adequate blinding, and comparator groups that reflect current best practices or account for the additional attention provided during exercise interventions.
